summary: Describes a method for encapsulating AX.25 frames, the amateur packet-radio link-layer protocol, within IP packets. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1226 places each AX.25 amateur packet-radio frame inside an IP datagram. It removes the HDLC framing that IP already replaces as a boundary marker and keeps the AX.25 frame check sequence.

how to send ax.25 over internet
how are ax.25 frames carried in ip
subtitle: A method for carrying AX.25 amateur packet-radio frames inside IP datagrams.

tldr.problem: AX.25 frames needed a defined way to travel inside Internet Protocol datagrams.
tldr.mechanism: Each AX.25 frame is carried in one IP datagram using IP protocol number 93; HDLC framing flags and zero-stuffing are omitted, while the frame check sequence is kept.
tldr.outcome: This document describes an experimental encapsulation method; it does not discuss security issues.

today: RFC 1226 is an Experimental protocol document. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Carrying AX.25 in IP
sections.content:
AX.25 is an Amateur Packet-Radio Link-Layer Protocol. RFC 1226 describes how to encapsulate its frames within IP datagrams.

Each AX.25 frame is placed in one IP datagram, which uses protocol number 93. A typical AX.25 frame normally does not exceed 330 octets, so IP fragmentation should not be necessary in the usual case.
sections.plainLanguage: One AX.25 frame goes inside one IP datagram. The IP protocol number identifies the datagram as carrying an AX.25 frame.

sections.title: What the Encapsulation Keeps
sections.content:
When an AX.25 frame is put in an IP datagram, the HDLC framing elements (flags and zero-stuffing) are omitted. The IP datagram marks the start and end of the encapsulated frame.

The 16-bit CRC-CCITT frame check sequence is included. In all other respects, the AX.25 frame is encapsulated unaltered. Larger experimental frame sizes may require standard IP fragmentation and reassembly.
sections.plainLanguage: IP supplies the outer boundary, so the HDLC flags and zero-stuffing are left out. The frame's 16-bit check sequence remains inside.

sections.title: Protocol Number and Scope
sections.content:
Every IP datagram that carries an AX.25 frame uses protocol number 93. The RFC refers readers to the AX.25 Amateur Packet-Radio Link-Layer Protocol Version 2.0 for the frame format itself.

The document says that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocol number 93 identifies IP datagrams containing AX.25 frames. The AX.25 reference document defines the frame protocol.

references.text: AX.25 Amateur Packet-Radio Link-Layer Protocol Version 2.0, October 1984. American Radio Relay League.
